content.problem: Provisioning and launching a TPU VM is only half the engineering job: if you pick the wrong TPU generation or miscalculate parameter + optimizer + KV-cache HBM bytes, your TPU experiment will either fail with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory` or under-utilize the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU).
content.idea: Budget capacity with a byte ledger before selecting a TPU slice, and treat the roofline ridge point as a theoretical screening estimate. GiB capacity and FLOP/byte ridge points are different quantities and must be read in separate panels. The worked training-state estimates state their tensor dtypes and exclusions; they are not observed runtime memory.
objectives: Compare Google Cloud TPU generations (`v5e`, `v5p`, `v6e` Trillium, and Ironwood) by HBM capacity, HBM bandwidth, and MXU BF16 throughput.
Calculate the Roofline ridge point (`bf16_tflops / bw_gbs`) in FLOPs per byte for each TPU generation.
Compute training-state and KV-cache HBM from explicit tensor byte counts, including master weights, compute weights, gradients, and Adam moments.
Make per-device training-state sizing decisions for replicated or explicitly sharded placement, then size inference KV cache separately with headroom.

sections.title: Connect MXU arithmetic intensity and HBM capacity to TPU slice sizing
sections.body:
Use a per-chip ledger before choosing a slice. In the exercise, 7B parameters with the stated mixed-BF16 accounting require 117.347 GiB of training state. Under ideal even sharding, four v6e chips need 29.33675 GiB per chip, above the fixture's 25.6 GiB usable budget at 80% of 32 GiB, so this plan fails before activations. Eight chips need 14.668375 GiB per chip, leaving 10.931625 GiB for activations and temporaries; with the assumed 8 GiB allowance it fits this arithmetic screen. This is a placement assumption, not proof that the implementation shards optimizer state evenly. Verify actual sharding and peak memory before reserving hardware.

Keep inference separate: the fixture's 7B BF16 KV cache at 8192 tokens is 1 GiB. Do not add it to the training-state total unless the workload actually runs training and inference together. The ridge point is peak BF16 throughput divided by HBM bandwidth, a theoretical roofline balance in FLOP/byte, not observed speed. Use it to form a profile hypothesis, then decide from a target trace whether compute, memory traffic or communication needs attention.

check.prompt: For 7 billion parameters, how many GiB does the stated 18-byte mixed-BF16 ledger require before activations, and why is a ridge point not a measured bottleneck?
check.answer: The estimate is 7e9 × 18 / 2^30 ≈ 117.4 GiB. It excludes activations, communication buffers, allocator overhead and temporary copies, so it is only a capacity lower bound. The ridge point compares published peak compute and bandwidth; only a workload measurement and profile can identify an observed bottleneck.

sections.math: B_{\text{state/device}} = \begin{cases} B_{\text{state}}, & \text{replicated} \\ B_{\text{state}}/N_{\text{chips}}, & \text{ideal even sharding} \end{cases}; \quad B_{\text{usable/device}} = f_{\text{usable}} B_{\text{HBM/chip}} - B_{\text{activation/device}}

sections.title: 1. Compare TPU generations (`v5e`, `v5p`, `v6e`, Ironwood) and calculate HBM budgets
sections.body:
The specification table provides per-chip capacity and bandwidth inputs for a first estimate; it does not promise availability, fit or workload speed. For the named v5e example, four chips have 64 GiB aggregate HBM, but the 48 GiB state still needs either 48 GiB on every chip if replicated or 12 GiB per chip under ideal even sharding. At the fixture's 80% usable allowance, each 16 GiB chip offers 12.8 GiB; adding 1 GiB of assumed activations makes the ideal shard 13 GiB and misses by 0.2 GiB. This is why aggregate slice capacity is not the fit test.

For each candidate, state the physical chip count, per-chip HBM budget, placement assumption and activation/temporary allowance. For the later v6e exercise, four chips fail the 7B mixed-BF16 estimate before activations, while eight leave room for the stated 8 GiB allowance. Keep inference KV cache as a separate workload budget. Select a topology only after checking real per-device placement and a target memory trace.

sections.title: Use chip specifications without confusing them with a runtime contract
sections.body: Treat physical chips, JAX devices and host processes as separate counts. Specifications describe per-chip resources; the selected machine type and API determine hosts and physical chips, while the runtime receipt reports observed processes and JAX devices. The TPU7x example in this lesson maps two JAX devices to one chip, so multiplying every JAX device count by per-chip HBM would overstate the physical capacity. Record API, machine type, requested topology and observed inventory together, and use the matching mapping when translating a device plan into a per-chip ledger. Peak throughput is a hardware ceiling, not evidence that a JAX expression uses that path.

content.code:
# Step 1 — Define TPU generation specs and compute Roofline ridge points
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np

TPU_SPECS = [
    {"gen": "v5e", "hbm_gib": 16.0, "bw_gbs": 819.0, "bf16_tflops": 197.0},
    {"gen": "v5p", "hbm_gib": 95.0, "bw_gbs": 2765.0, "bf16_tflops": 459.0},
    {"gen": "v6e", "hbm_gib": 32.0, "bw_gbs": 1638.0, "bf16_tflops": 918.0},
]
for s in TPU_SPECS:
    s["ridge_flops_per_byte"] = round((s["bf16_tflops"] * 1e12) / (s["bw_gbs"] * 1e9), 1)


# Step 2 — Estimate training-state and KV-cache HBM budgets across precisions
def estimate_memory_gib(params_billions, kv_tokens, layers=32, kv_heads=8, head_dim=128):
    n_params = params_billions * 1e9
    kv_elements = 2.0 * layers * kv_tokens * kv_heads * head_dim
    gib = float(1024 ** 3)
    return {
        "fp32_train_state_gib": round((n_params * 16.0) / gib, 3),
        "mixed_bf16_train_state_gib": round((n_params * 18.0) / gib, 3),
        "kv_fp32_gib": round((kv_elements * 4.0) / gib, 3),
        "kv_bf16_gib": round((kv_elements * 2.0) / gib, 3),
        "kv_int8_gib": round((kv_elements * 1.0) / gib, 3),
    }


def per_device_hbm_ledger(total_state_gib, chips, chip_hbm_gib, placement, usable_fraction=0.8, activation_gib_per_chip=0.0):
    if chips < 1 or not 0 < usable_fraction <= 1 or activation_gib_per_chip < 0:
        raise ValueError("chips and utilization must be positive; activation allowance cannot be negative")
    if placement == "replicated":
        state_per_chip = float(total_state_gib)
    elif placement == "evenly_sharded_ideal":
        state_per_chip = float(total_state_gib) / chips
    else:
        raise ValueError("placement must be replicated or evenly_sharded_ideal")
    usable_hbm_per_chip = float(chip_hbm_gib) * usable_fraction
    available_for_state = usable_hbm_per_chip - activation_gib_per_chip
    return {"placement_assumption": placement, "chips": chips, "state_per_chip_gib": state_per_chip,
            "activation_allowance_per_chip_gib": activation_gib_per_chip,
            "usable_hbm_per_chip_gib": usable_hbm_per_chip,
            "fits_under_assumptions": state_per_chip <= available_for_state,
            "remaining_after_state_before_activation_gib": usable_hbm_per_chip - state_per_chip}



budget_7b = estimate_memory_gib(params_billions=7.0, kv_tokens=8192)
budget_1p5b = estimate_memory_gib(params_billions=1.5, kv_tokens=4096)
assert budget_7b["mixed_bf16_train_state_gib"] > 64.0 and budget_7b["mixed_bf16_train_state_gib"] < 128.0
# Assert invariant `budget_1p5b["mixed_bf16_train_state_gib"] < 64.0` holds
assert budget_1p5b["mixed_bf16_train_state_gib"] < 64.0
print("TPU ridge points (FLOP/byte):", {s["gen"]: s["ridge_flops_per_byte"] for s in TPU_SPECS})
print("7B memory budget (GiB):", budget_7b)
print("1.5B memory budget (GiB):", budget_1p5b)

# Experiment — Compare KV-cache memory across FP32, BF16, and INT8
assert np.isclose(budget_7b["kv_fp32_gib"], 2.0 * budget_7b["kv_bf16_gib"])
assert np.isclose(budget_7b["kv_bf16_gib"], 2.0 * budget_7b["kv_int8_gib"])

experiments.title: Estimate minimum v5e chips under ideal even sharding
experiments.prediction: Under even state sharding and an 80% per-chip HBM budget, what is the arithmetic minimum number of 16 GiB v5e chips? What would a supported 16-chip request leave per chip before activations?
experiments.code:
state_gib = budget_7b["mixed_bf16_train_state_gib"]
usable_gib_per_chip = 16.0 * 0.8
minimum_ideal_chips = int(np.ceil(state_gib / usable_gib_per_chip))
state_per_chip_on_16 = state_gib / 16
remaining_before_activations = usable_gib_per_chip - state_per_chip_on_16
print("Ideal-sharding arithmetic minimum:", minimum_ideal_chips)
print("At 16 chips, state/device GiB:", state_per_chip_on_16, "remaining before activations:", remaining_before_activations)
assert minimum_ideal_chips == 10
assert state_per_chip_on_16 < usable_gib_per_chip
assert remaining_before_activations > 0
experiments.output: The arithmetic lower bound is 10 chips if the entire 117.347 GiB state is evenly sharded. The illustrative 16-chip v5e layout needs about 7.33 GiB/device, leaving about 5.47 GiB/device below the 80% budget for all activations and temporary buffers.
experiments.explanation: This is only a capacity bound under ideal even sharding, not a proof of a 10-chip supported slice or of actual placement. The selected Cloud TPU API/GKE topology determines which slice shapes exist. Verify parameter and optimizer-state shardings, plus peak activations and temporary memory, before launch.

experiments.title: Decide between replicated and sharded placement with headroom
experiments.prediction: Does a 48 GiB state fit per 16 GiB v5e chip when replicated, ideally sharded over four chips, and when each chip also needs 1 GiB for activations? What changes at 52 GiB?
experiments.code:
replicated = per_device_hbm_ledger(48, 4, 16, "replicated", activation_gib_per_chip=1)
ideal_shard = per_device_hbm_ledger(48, 4, 16, "evenly_sharded_ideal", activation_gib_per_chip=1)
changed = per_device_hbm_ledger(52, 4, 16, "evenly_sharded_ideal", activation_gib_per_chip=1)
print("Per-chip ledgers:", replicated, ideal_shard, changed)
assert replicated["state_per_chip_gib"] == 48.0 and not replicated["fits_under_assumptions"]
assert ideal_shard["state_per_chip_gib"] == 12.0 and not ideal_shard["fits_under_assumptions"]
assert changed["state_per_chip_gib"] == 13.0 and not changed["fits_under_assumptions"]
experiments.output: Replication requires 48 GiB/device and fails. Ideal sharding requires 12 GiB/device, but with a 1 GiB activation allowance it exceeds the 12.8 GiB usable budget; 52 GiB sharded requires 13 GiB/device and fails before activations.
experiments.explanation: This is conditional on placement. Confirm array shardings and optimizer-state placement before treating the ideal-sharded estimate as a fit.

content.exercise: For a 7B mixed-BF16 training state, compare ideal evenly sharded v6e-4 and v6e-8 plans at 80% HBM per chip. Report per-chip state and remaining HBM before activations, then decide whether each can fit under an additional 8 GiB/device activation-and-temporary allowance. Separately report the BF16 inference KV cache at 8192 tokens. State the placement assumption and do not add inference KV cache to training state.
content.solution:
state = budget_7b["mixed_bf16_train_state_gib"]
for chips in (4, 8):
    ledger = per_device_hbm_ledger(state, chips, 32.0, "evenly_sharded_ideal", activation_gib_per_chip=8.0)
    print("v6e chips:", chips, "state/device GiB:", ledger["state_per_chip_gib"], "usable GiB:", ledger["usable_hbm_per_chip_gib"], "fits with assumed activation:", ledger["fits_under_assumptions"])
    assert ledger["fits_under_assumptions"] is (chips == 8)
print("Separate inference BF16 KV cache GiB:", budget_7b["kv_bf16_gib"])
assert np.isclose(budget_7b["kv_bf16_gib"], 1.0)

content.question: What does the theoretical BF16 Roofline ridge point, \(1000 \times \text{TFLOP/s} / \text{GB/s}\) in FLOP/byte, describe?
options: How many SSH keys can connect to the TPU VM
The arithmetic intensity where the ideal HBM-bandwidth ceiling meets the ideal BF16-compute ceiling
How long `gcloud compute tpus tpu-vm create` takes to provision
content.explanation: Convert both rates to FLOP/s and byte/s first. The ratio locates the intersection of two ideal ceilings. Below it the bandwidth ceiling is lower; above it the compute ceiling is lower. Actual performance can fall below either ceiling because of tiling, communication, vector work or launch overhead.
content.diagnosis: If your TPU job fails with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED: Out of memory while trying to allocate...`, compare your parameter + optimizer + activation + KV-cache byte estimate against per-chip HBM (`16` GiB on `v5e`, `32` GiB on `v6e`) and shard the state across chips (`NamedSharding` / FSDP) or reduce microbatch size.
takeaways: Size your TPU slice (`v5e`, `v5p`, `v6e`) from explicit HBM byte budgets for training state and KV caches before launching.
Use the Roofline comparison to propose a bottleneck hypothesis, then check actual target traces, traffic, precision and synchronized timing before choosing fusion, quantization or a tile.

visual.title: TPU capacity, ridge point and per-device placement bounds
visual.prediction: How do per-chip HBM capacity (GiB) and the compute-to-memory ridge point (FLOP/byte) change across TPU `v5e`, `v5p`, and `v6e`?
visual.reading:
The first panel's vertical axis is HBM per physical chip in GiB: v5e 16, v5p 95 and v6e 32. The second is theoretical BF16 ridge point in FLOP/byte: 240.5, 166.0 and 560.4. v5p has more per-chip HBM than v6e but a lower ridge point; a larger ridge value means more arithmetic per HBM byte is needed to reach the compute ceiling, not that the workload is faster. In the third panel, the 48 GiB state on four v5e chips is 48 GiB/device if replicated and 12 GiB/device if ideally sharded, against 12.8 GiB/device usable. Adding the fixture's 1 GiB activation allowance makes the shard 13 GiB and exceeds budget by 0.2 GiB. Choose smaller state, more chips or a validated placement, then check measured peak memory.

These are calculated capacity scenarios, not device measurements.
visual.connection: These are specification and fixture calculations, not measured target behavior. The first two panels compare hardware capacity and roofline balance; the third makes the placement decision explicit. The later 7B mixed-BF16 exercise estimates 29.33675 GiB/device on four v6e chips versus a 25.6 GiB usable budget, while eight chips need 14.668375 GiB/device and leave 10.931625 GiB before activations. Its assumed 8 GiB allowance fits arithmetically. Confirm actual sharding and live peak memory before selecting a slice; assess the separate 1 GiB BF16 inference KV cache only for inference.

diagram.prediction: What remains on each physical chip under replication versus explicit sharding, and where do BF16 operands enter?
diagram.reading: Follow the arrows from the per-device HBM ledger, through operand traffic, into the chosen compute path, and finally to a target trace. The ledger must name placement: for 48 GiB of state on four 16 GiB v5e chips, replication needs 48 GiB/device; ideal even sharding needs 12 GiB/device. With the fixture's 1 GiB activation allowance, that shard needs 13 GiB against 12.8 GiB usable, so it misses by 0.2 GiB. The bandwidth node carries GB/s figures, while the compute comparison is in FLOP/byte; inspect each unit on its own. Inference KV cache is a separate ledger. The next step is to confirm actual sharding and inspect a target trace for memory, compute and communication evidence.
diagram.alt: Conceptual TPU per-device ledger: replicated training state is copied to every chip; explicitly sharded state is partitioned across chips; activations and temporaries use additional HBM; a separate inference path holds KV cache; BF16 operands stream from HBM to compute.

optionFeedback: A roofline ratio describes compute and memory rates. Authentication and SSH limits belong to a different control-plane contract.

Convert both rates to FLOP/s and byte/s first. The ratio locates the intersection of two ideal ceilings. Below it the bandwidth ceiling is lower; above it the compute ceiling is lower. Actual performance can fall below either ceiling because of tiling, communication, vector work or launch overhead.
Provisioning wait depends on capacity and scheduling, not this compute-to-bandwidth ratio. Keep capacity planning separate from kernel analysis.
